subject: basking lizard
title: What If Humans Were Cold-Blooded Like Lizards?

scenes.text: What if you were cold-blooded? You'd eat a tenth as much. Mornings would be the problem.
A resting reptile burns 10 to 20 percent of the energy of a same-sized mammal, under a tenth of the food.
So you could skip meals for months. Big crocodiles go over a year between meals.
But your temperature follows the air. Cold morning? You'd lie basking, too sluggish to move, like a crocodile.
And forget long runs. Cold-blooded muscle works mostly without oxygen: three to five minutes flat out, then hours to recover.
A resting mammal uses as much oxygen as a sprinting reptile. Warm blood costs ten times the food. It buys you the day.

description:
What if humans were cold-blooded? A resting reptile uses only 10 to 20 percent of the energy of a bird or mammal of the same size, and needs less than a tenth of the food per kilogram; large crocodiles can go more than a year without eating. But an ectotherm's body temperature follows its surroundings, so a cold morning means basking before you can move, and its muscles rely mostly on anaerobic metabolism: three to five minutes of maximum effort, then hours of recovery. A mammal at rest consumes about as much oxygen as a reptile at full exertion.

first_comment: A Burmese python's heart grows 40 percent within two days of a big meal, then shrinks back. Would you trade three meals a day for one a month?
